title: Coulomb's law (magnitude of electrostatic force)
body: \left|\vec F_E\right| = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2} = k\frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}
ced_evidence: 10.1.A.2 "Coulomb's law describes the electrostatic force between two charged objects as directly proportional to the magnitude of each of the charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance"

title: Direction of the electrostatic force
body: The electrostatic force lies along the line of separation between the objects; like charges repel and opposite charges attract.
ced_evidence: 10.1.A.3, 10.1.A.3.i, 10.1.A.3.ii "parallel to the line of separation"

title: Charges of the basic particles
body: The elementary charge e is the smallest indivisible amount of charge, and the three basic particles carry these charges.
ced_evidence: 10.1.A.1.ii, 10.1.A.1.iii "The charge of an electron is −e, the charge of a proton is +e, and a neutron has no electric charge"

title: Point charge
body: A point charge is a model in which the physical size of a charged object or system is negligible in the context of the situation being analyzed.
ced_evidence: 10.1.A.1.iv "A point charge is a model in which the physical size of a charged object or system is negligible"

title: Electric vs. gravitational force comparison
body: Electrostatic forces can be attractive or repulsive while gravity is always attractive; gravity is usually far weaker between charged masses but dominates at large scales because large systems tend to be electrically neutral.
ced_evidence: 10.1.B.1, 10.1.B.2, 10.1.B.3 "gravitational forces are always attractive"

title: Electric permittivity and polarization
body: Electric permittivity measures the degree to which a material or medium is polarized in an electric field, where polarization is the induced rearrangement of electrons that separates positive and negative charge; free space has the constant value ε₀.
ced_evidence: 10.1.C.1, 10.1.C.2, 10.1.C.3 "Electric permittivity is a measurement of the degree to which a material or medium is polarized"

title: Conductors and insulators
body: Conductors are made of materials in which charge carriers move easily, while insulators are made of materials in which charge carriers cannot move easily.
ced_evidence: 10.1.C.4.ii "Conductors are made from electrically conducting materials in which charge carriers move easily"

title: Conservation of charge and charging
body: A system's net charge stays constant unless charge, typically electrons, is transferred to or from it, as by friction or contact.
ced_evidence: 10.2.A.2.i, 10.2.A.2.ii "The net charge of a system will be constant unless there is a transfer of charge to or from the system"

title: Induced charge separation
body: Induced charge separation occurs when the electrostatic force between two systems alters the distribution of charges within them, polarizing one or both, and it can occur in neutral systems.
ced_evidence: 10.2.A.1.ii, 10.2.A.1.iii "Induced charge separation occurs when the electrostatic force between two systems alters the distribution of charges"

title: Grounding
body: Grounding is electrically connecting a charged system to a much larger, approximately neutral system such as Earth.
ced_evidence: 10.2.A.3 "Grounding involves electrically connecting a charged system to a much larger and approximately neutral system"

title: Electric field definition
body: \vec E = \frac{\vec F_E}{q}
ced_evidence: 10.3.A.2 "The electric field at a given point is the ratio of the electric force exerted on a test charge at that point to the charge of the test charge"

title: Field magnitude of a point charge
body: |\vec E| = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{|q|}{r^2} = k\frac{|q|}{r^2}
ced_evidence: 10.3.A.2 and 10.1.A.2 combined; 10.3.B.1.ii "the same as the electric field due to a point charge"

title: Test charge
body: A test charge is a point charge of small enough magnitude that its presence does not significantly affect the electric field in its vicinity.
ced_evidence: 10.3.A.2.i "A test charge is a point charge of small enough magnitude"

title: Direction of the electric field
body: An electric field points away from isolated positive charges and toward isolated negative charges, and the force on a positive test charge is in the field's direction.
ced_evidence: 10.3.A.2.ii, 10.3.A.2.iii "points away from isolated positive charges and toward isolated negative charges"

title: Net electric field is a vector sum
body: The net electric field at a location is the vector sum of the individual fields created by nearby charged objects.
ced_evidence: 10.3.A.3.i "the vector sum of individual electric fields"

title: Electric field map and field line diagram
body: Field maps use vectors, and field line diagrams are simplified models of them, to show the relative magnitude and direction of the field at positions in a region.

items.label: Field vector
items.meaning: arrow showing the field's magnitude and direction at a location

items.label: Field line
items.meaning: line showing direction; the spacing of lines indicates relative magnitude

items.label: Source charges
items.meaning: lines or vectors point away from positive and toward negative charges

ced_evidence: 10.3.A.3.ii, 10.3.A.3.iii "Electric field line diagrams are simplified models of electric field maps"

title: Charged conductors in electrostatic equilibrium
body: Excess charge on a solid conductor sits on its surface, the field inside is zero, the field at the surface is perpendicular to it, and outside an isolated spherically symmetric sphere the field equals that of a point charge at its center.
ced_evidence: 10.3.B.1, 10.3.B.1.i, 10.3.B.1.ii "the electric field within the conductor is zero"

title: Charged insulators in electrostatic equilibrium
body: Excess charge on an insulator is distributed throughout its interior as well as its surface, and the field inside may be nonzero (qualitative analysis only).
ced_evidence: 10.3.B.2 "the electric field within the insulator may have a nonzero value"

title: Electric potential energy of two point charges
body: U_E = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\frac{q_1 q_2}{r} = k\frac{q_1 q_2}{r}
caution: Keep the signs of q₁ and q₂ here; unlike Coulomb's force magnitude, U_E can be negative.
ced_evidence: 10.4.A.2 "The general form for the electric potential energy of two charged objects"

title: Electric potential energy of a two-charge system
body: The electric potential energy of a system of two point charges equals the work an external force must do to bring the charges to their current positions from infinitely far away.
ced_evidence: 10.4.A.1 "the amount of work required for an external force to bring the point charges to their current positions from infinitely far away"

title: Total potential energy is a sum over pairs
body: The total electric potential energy of a system is the sum of the potential energies of each pair of charged objects (four or fewer point charges required).
ced_evidence: 10.4.A.3 "the sum of the electric potential energies of the individual interactions between each pair"

title: Electric potential
body: Electric potential is the electric potential energy per unit charge at a point in space.
ced_evidence: 10.5.A.1 "Electric potential describes the electric potential energy per unit charge at a point in space"

title: Electric potential of point charges (scalar superposition)
body: V = \frac{1}{4\pi\varepsilon_0}\sum_i \frac{q_i}{r_i} = k\sum_i \frac{q_i}{r_i}
caution: Potential is a scalar, so add the terms algebraically with signs; do not add vectors.
ced_evidence: 10.5.A.2 "principle of scalar superposition of the electric potential due to each of the point charges"

title: Electric potential difference
body: \Delta V = \frac{\Delta U_E}{q}
ced_evidence: 10.5.A.3 "the change in electric potential energy per unit charge when a test charge is moved between the two points"

title: Conductors in contact share potential
body: When conductors are in electrical contact, electrons redistribute until the conductors' surfaces are at the same electric potential; a battery also produces a potential difference by chemically separating charge.
ced_evidence: 10.5.A.4, 10.5.A.3.i "the surfaces of the conductors are at the same electric potential"

title: Average field from potential difference
body: |\vec E_{avg}| = \frac{|\Delta V|}{\Delta r}
ced_evidence: 10.5.B.1 "The average electric field between two points in space is equal to the electric potential difference between the two points divided by the distance"

title: Equipotential lines and field direction rules
body: Isolines of electric potential are perpendicular to the field vectors, the field points toward decreasing potential, and the field has no component along an isoline.
ced_evidence: 10.5.B.2.i–iv "Isolines are perpendicular to electric field vectors"

title: Equipotential (isoline) map
body: An isoline map of electric potential can be built from an electric field vector map, and the field map from an isoline map, to predict the motion of charged objects.

items.label: Field vectors
items.meaning: drawn perpendicular to isolines, pointing toward decreasing potential

items.label: Spacing
items.meaning: closer isolines mean a stronger average field

ced_evidence: 10.5.B.2, 10.5.B.2.ii "An isoline map of electric potential can be constructed from an electric field vector map"

title: Parallel-plate capacitor
body: A parallel-plate capacitor consists of two separated parallel conducting surfaces that can hold equal amounts of charge with opposite signs.
ced_evidence: 10.6.A.1 "two separated parallel conducting surfaces that can hold equal amounts of charge with opposite signs"

title: Capacitance definition
body: C = \frac{Q}{\Delta V}
ced_evidence: 10.6.A.2 "Capacitance relates the magnitude of the charge stored on each plate to the electric potential difference"

title: Parallel-plate capacitance
body: C = \frac{\kappa \varepsilon_0 A}{d}
ced_evidence: 10.6.A.2.ii "proportional to the area of one of its plates and inversely proportional to the distance between its plates"

title: Field between charged parallel plates
body: E_C = \frac{Q}{\kappa \varepsilon_0 A}
ced_evidence: 10.6.A.3.i "The magnitude of the electric field between two charged parallel plates"

title: Uniform field and motion between plates
body: Between charged parallel plates the field is constant in magnitude and direction except near the edges, so a charged particle undergoes constant acceleration like projectile motion in Earth's gravitational field.
ced_evidence: 10.6.A.3, 10.6.A.3.ii "undergoes constant acceleration"

title: Energy stored in a capacitor
body: U_C = \tfrac{1}{2} Q \Delta V
ced_evidence: 10.6.A.5 "The electric potential energy stored in a capacitor is described by the equation"

title: Effect of a dielectric
body: Adding a dielectric between the plates changes the capacitance and induces a field in the dielectric opposite in direction to the field between the plates.
ced_evidence: 10.6.A.6 "induces an electric field in the dielectric in the opposite direction to the field between the plates"

title: Change in electric potential energy of a charge
body: \Delta U_E = q\,\Delta V
ced_evidence: 10.7.A.1 "the resulting change in the electric potential energy of the object-field system"

title: Energy conservation for a charge moving through a potential difference
body: A charged object moving between points of different potential changes its kinetic energy consistently with conservation of energy, so ΔK = −ΔU_E for the object-field system.
ced_evidence: 10.7.A.2 "a change in kinetic energy of the object consistent with the conservation of energy"
